I wish there was a beginners DCG section since this may be pretty elementary.

Also since the DCG section has been a bit slow, it might be worth throwing out an easy one.

I was talking to Bob Hess some weeks ago. I mentioned I was getting my MG 457nm laser soon (this Friday ). He said I might get brighter holograms as a result of using blue light as opposed to green (400mw of blue vs. 100mw of green, I am guessing about 10X to 20X more sensitive). When I asked why, he said that (this is not a quote, just bad memory talking) the stronger sensitivity hence shorter exposure time would result in a stronger bond. That is, if the DCG exposed quickly, than the crosslinking would be stronger, perhaps even deeper. 

I've been pondering this for a while now. I know some materials do make stronger bonds when exposed to high pulse light, but not sure if this is true with DCG. If this is the case, would it be even stronger if you have a blue pulse laser?

Any comments from the DCG gurus?

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **BobH:** As far as I know, pulsed lasers won't work with DCG because there isn't enough time durring the exposure for the molecules to do anything.

There have been successful attempts with pulsed lasers – the last one I am aware of was described in Jeff's 2006 paper, Improving the remarkable photosensitivity of dichromated gelatin for hologram recording in green laser light:

*... the energy used to make that single pulse image of living fingers was apparently as low as 12mJ per cm2.*

Even dye-sensitized DCG (“MB-DCG” etc.) might work with pulsed lasers...

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **BobH:** I was just thinking that since DCG is naturally more sensitive to blue light, that the resulting shorter exposure times means less chance of movement or other environmentally caused problems durring the exposure.

In my opinion, that's the gist of it, Tony.

I don't think there's anything mysterious about blue light in this respect. In all holograms, we want maximum edge acuity between exposed and unexposed areas. Whenever the material is more sensitive, it allows for shorter exposure times, thus making it a lot easier to produce good, bright holograms.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Well here is another thought based on my initial response.

My initial response:

> I would have to say it is due to properties that gelatin hardens with light. Thus with longer exposures the gel is hardening as it is being developed. With shorter exposure times, all bonds are pretty much make at the same time without the gel changing properties too much during exposure.

The key here to remember is DCG exposes quickly in the beginning and more slowly near the end of optimal exposure.

Another effect is based on looking at the light struck fringe and the supposedly non light struck fringe. We have to assume we are using a diffusing, randomly polarizing object. We also have to keep in mind that as we expose the AmDi is being used up and a lot of crosslinking happens in the beginning of exposure then just a little toward the end. Near the end of the optimal exposure when most AmDi is used up and most crosslinking has already happened we get a very slow reaction (hardening).

Now, with a short exposure, the optimal exposure time is reached for the light struck fringe while keeping the incorrectly polarizing light that hits the destructive fringe from hardening it too much. Remember, the destructive area is getting very little light that is not amplifying at all with the reference beam. So not much hardening has happened there. At least not in a short time period.

With a long exposure, we are allowing the incorrectly polarized light that is hitting the destructive fringe ample time to harden it. In a 120 second exposure, the last 60 seconds of exposure is needed to get the constructive fringe it's last 20 or so optimally hardened amount allowing the destructive area ample time to use up more AmDi and get more hardened because there is so much AmDi still left and it is still in the beginning stages of crosslinking relatively quickly.

Does this make sense? If not, I can try to plot it I guess.

2.	with the green the overall hardness is not met and chrome level is high that a fixer is need to remove the chrome and harden it just enough to clear the exposed areas and clear milkyness meeting the overall hardness for a one min soak time .

3.	And filling the sponge (gel) with just enough water to process the hologram and controlling that process by time and temp (cold water). I do remember reading that there was testing using steam to process the dcg hologram, buy holding the hologram in the steam till you see the relief there by swelling the gel just enough . in this process you can see in the one min or shorter a relief in the gel
